newsitem.title: CROATIA: Soros society trial to open in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Soros society trial to open in Croatia.

text.p: An international humanitarian foundation sponsored by U.S. tycoon George Soros will be taken to court by Croatia on Wednesday in what foundation officials say is a politically motivated and legally unfounded process.

Croatian financial police in December raided the premises of the Soros foundation's branch in Zagreb, The Open Society, and said it found evidence of "illegal financial transactions" allegedly carried out by the society during the previous year.
The Society was accused of financial malpractice and tax evasion of some $500,000 and the Zagreb public prosecutor indicted three senior Society officials on charges of falsifying financial records.

Cedo Prodanovic, a lawyer and member of the defence team, told a news conference in Zagreb on Tuesday the indictment was "the result of various factors, initiated by the speech by (Croatian) President Franjo Tudjman and his attack on the Open Society and George Soros".
In November the nationalist president branded as an enemy of the state the Hungarian-born businessman and philanthropist who champions democratic reform in former communist countries.
Shortly after that, police confiscated $65,000 from two of the indicted officials at a border crossing.
"The demonisation of the Society took a concrete form after the speech," said Prodanovic's defence colleague Slobodan Budak.
Prodanovic said the authorities' treatment of the Society since November, including the raid on the premises, was an abuse of the Croatian judiciary system.

Budak said the Open Society was not a legal entity and was therefore not subject to criminal prosecution. It was a branch of an international humanitarian organisation and was duly registered with the authorities, he added.
"Formally and legally I see no possibility of them being found guilty," Budak told reporters.
The Society in January paid the authorities $500,000 for alleged overdue taxes, "upon insistance of George Soros himself," said Karmen Basic, the Society's director.
But a spokeswoman said it did not mean "we admit the guilt, only that we want to be in compliance with tax laws."
